title: Orbital Trauma & Blow-out Fractures: A Comprehensive Clinical Guide
summary: This visual guide details the diagnosis and management of orbital trauma, specifically focusing on lid lacerations and the clinical complexities of orbital floor blow-out fractures, including diagnostic signs, diplopia mechanisms, and surgical criteria.

sections.title: Introduction to Orbital Floor Blow-out Fractures

branches: Mechanism: Sudden increase in orbital pressure from an impacting object (e.g., fist, tennis ball) > 5 cm (orbital aperture diameter).
Impact Dynamics: Eyeball is displaced and transmits rather than absorbs the impact (Fig. 22.5A).
Location: Most frequently involves the floor along the thin bone covering the infraorbital canal; medial wall occasionally involved.
Resistance: Lateral wall and roof are usually able to withstand such trauma.
Systemic Care: Ensure full evaluation for head and systemic injury; initiate necessary interspecialty referrals.

rows: Visual Function
Visual acuity should be recorded and monitored.
Periocular Signs
Variable ecchymosis, oedema, and occasionally subcutaneous emphysema (crackling sensation on palpation due to air in subcutaneous tissues).
Sensory Deficit
Infraorbital nerve anaesthesia: involves lower lid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, upper teeth, and gums (common due to infraorbital canal involvement).
Ocular Damage
Exclude hyphaema, angle recession, and retinal dialysis (relatively uncommon in blow-out fractures).
Enophthalmos
Manifests after oedema resolves (a few days). Late enophthalmos is uncommon; only 20% of large fractures have >2mm enophthalmos at 6 months (Fig. 22.6B).

sections.title: Mechanisms of Diplopia
content: 1. Haemorrhage and Oedema: Tightening of septa connecting inferior rectus/oblique to periorbita restricts movement. Usually improves as swelling resolves.

2. Mechanical Entrapment: Entrapment of inferior rectus, inferior oblique, or adjacent connective tissue/fat within the fracture (Fig. 22.6D). Causes diplopia in both upgaze (Fig. 22.6A & C) and downgaze.
3. Direct Muscle Injury: Associated with a negative forced duction test. Muscle fibres usually regenerate with normal function returning within ~2 months.

sections.title: Diagnostic Tests for Restricted Motility
content: Forced Duction Test: Positive in mechanical entrapment.
Differential Intraocular Pressure Test: Positive (IOP increases as a restricted muscle presses on the globe).
Hess Chart Testing: Useful to map eye movements, assess, and monitor (Fig. 22.7).
Hess Chart (Fig. 22.7): Shows restriction of left upgaze (SR and IO) and downgaze (IR) with secondary overaction of the right eye.

sections.title: Imaging & Evaluation (CT Scan)
content: CT Coronal Sections: Essential for evaluating fracture extent (Fig. 22.8, Fig. 22.6D).
Tear Drop Sign: Soft tissue prolapse into the maxillary antrum (Fig. 22.8).
Antral Densities: May represent prolapsed orbital fat, extraocular muscles, haematoma, or unrelated antral polyps.

sections.title: Initial Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Observation and prescription of oral antibiotics.
Step 2: Application of ice packs and use of nasal decongestants.
Step 3: Patient Instruction: Do NOT blow nose (prevents forcing infected sinus contents into the orbit).
Step 4: Systemic Steroids: Occasionally required for severe orbital oedema, especially if compromising the optic nerve.

sections.title: URGENT RED FLAG: ‘White-eyed’ Fracture
content: Subgroup requiring URGENT repair to avoid permanent neuromuscular damage.
Patient Demographic: Generally < 18 years of age due to greater bone elasticity.
Clinical Presentation: Little visible external soft tissue injury (Fig. 22.6C).
Mechanism: 'Trap-door' effect causing acute incarceration of herniated tissue.
Systemic Symptoms: Acute nausea, vomiting, headache.
Risk: Persistent activation of the oculo-cardiac reflex.
CT Imaging: Features may be subtle.

rows: Small cracks without herniation
No treatment required (risk of permanent complications is small).
Fracture < 1/2 floor, no herniation/enophthalmos, improving diplopia
No treatment required.
Fracture > 1/2 floor
May develop enophthalmos if left untreated.
Entrapment, Enophthalmos > 2mm, or persistent diplopia in primary position
Repair within 2 weeks.
Enophthalmos < 2mm
No difference in outcome between surgery at 2 weeks vs 6 months.
Diplopia & tissue incarceration (no muscle entrapment)
Often improves without surgery; delayed surgery still effective (except in extreme upgaze).

sections.title: Surgical Repair Methods
content: 1. Incision Approach: Transconjunctival, subciliary, or via the maxillary sinus.
2. Periosteal Elevation: Elevation of the periosteum from the orbital floor.
3. Freeing Contents: Freeing of trapped orbital contents.
4. Reconstruction: Repair of the bony defect with a synthetic implant.

sections.title: Exhaustive Text Preservation Bloc
sections.content: CHAPTER 22 Trauma. Orbital Trauma (p. 911-912). Fig. 22.4 (A) Small upper lid laceration in a child showing the tip of a coloured pencil; (B) axial CT scan showing the broken tips (arrows); (C) penetrating injury to the left upper lid with an intact globe; (D) axial CT scan showing a retrobulbar glass shard. Diagnosis: Visual function, especially acuity, should be recorded and monitored. Orbital floor fracture Introduction: A blow-out fracture of the orbital floor is typically caused by a sudden increase in the orbital pressure from an impacting object that is greater in diameter than the orbital aperture (about 5 cm), such as a fist or tennis ball, so that the eyeball itself is displaced and transmits rather than absorbs the impact (Fig. 22.5A). Since the bones of the lateral wall and the roof are usually able to withstand such trauma, the fracture most frequently involves the floor of the orbit along the thin bone covering the infraorbital canal. Occasionally, the medial orbital wall may also be fractured. Fractures of the orbital rim and adjacent facial bones require appropriately tailored management. Clinical features vary with the severity of trauma and the interval between injury and examination. Care should be taken to ensure that a full evaluation for head and systemic injury has been performed and any necessary interspecialty referrals initiated. Periocular signs include variable ecchymosis, oedema (Fig. 22.5B) and occasionally subcutaneous emphysema (a crackling sensation on palpation due to air in the subcutaneous tissues). Infraorbital nerve anaesthesia involving the lower lid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, upper teeth and gums is common as the fracture frequently involves the infraorbital canal. Diplopia may be caused by: Haemorrhage and oedema causing tightening of septa connecting inferior rectus/oblique to periorbita; mechanical entrapment within the fracture (Fig. 22.6D); direct injury to muscle (negative forced duction). Forced duction and differential IOP tests are positive in entrapment. Enophthalmos manifests as oedema resolves; 20% of large fractures show >2mm at 6 months. Hess chart (Fig 22.7) maps eye movements. CT coronal sections (Fig 22.8) evaluate fracture extent and 'tear drop' sign. Initial Treatment: Observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, nasal decongestants. No nose blowing. Steroids for severe oedema. Subsequent Treatment aims to prevent permanent vertical diplopia/enophthalmos. Small cracks/minimal herniation do not require treatment. Fractures > 1/2 floor or with >2mm enophthalmos/persistent primary diplopia should be repaired within 2 weeks. 'White-eyed' fracture (under 18 years) requires urgent repair for tissue incarceration/trap-door effect; presents with nausea/vomiting. Surgical repair via transconjunctival, subciliary, or maxillary sinus with synthetic implant.
